title: 2 Samuel 15:1–12
context: Restored to Jerusalem but kept at a distance, Absalom builds a following by presenting himself as the people's champion at the city gate, undermining confidence in his father's justice. After winning hearts, he asks leave to fulfill a vow in Hebron, David's first capital, and there launches a planned revolt, drawing in David's trusted counselor Ahithophel. The rebellion unfolds against the background of Nathan's word that the sword would not depart from David's house (2 Samuel 12:10).

verses.text: After this, Absalom prepared a chariot and horses for himself, and fifty men to run before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom gathers a chariot, horses, and fifty runners. Arminian readers see a man freely choosing to grasp at power, cultivating the image of a king while his father still reigns, a real moral act with real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this display follows Nathan's warning that God would "raise up evil against you out of your own house" (12:11). Absalom's ambition is his own sin, and it also becomes the means of the discipline God announced.

verses.text: Absalom rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate. When any man had a suit which should come to the king for judgment, then Absalom called to him, and said, “What city are you from?” He said, “Your servant is of one of the tribes of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom rises early to intercept people bringing cases to the king. Arminian readers note his deliberate strategy: he exploits real frustrations, positioning himself between the people and the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Absalom targets the place of justice, the city gate. His scheme reveals a heart set on self-exaltation, and the narrative shows how sin can disguise itself as concern for others.

verses.text: Absalom said to him, “Behold, your matters are good and right; but there is no man deputized by the king to hear you.”
verses.arminianNotes: "There is no man deputized by the king to hear you." Arminian readers note that Absalom may be exploiting a real weakness in David's administration, while using it dishonestly to undermine his father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see a possible truth twisted into a lie. Flattery that tells everyone their case is right is not justice but manipulation, aimed at winning loyalty rather than serving righteousness.

verses.text: Absalom said moreover, “Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man who has any suit or cause might come to me, and I would do him justice!”
verses.arminianNotes: "Oh that I were made judge in the land." Arminian readers see naked ambition dressed as public service, a desire to rule that sets itself against God's appointed king and the order God established.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David was anointed by God (1 Samuel 16:13), so Absalom's wish is a challenge to God's own choice. They see in this a pattern of human pride seeking a throne God has not given.

verses.text: It was so, that when any man came near to bow down to him, he stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and kissed him.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom stops people from bowing and kisses them instead. Arminian readers note the calculated warmth: the gesture appears humble and generous, yet it serves to bind people to himself rather than to the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that David once kissed Absalom in reconciliation (14:33). Absalom now uses the same gesture to steal loyalty, showing how outward affection can mask betrayal.

verses.text: Absalom did this sort of thing to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: "So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." Arminian readers see the people as genuinely responsible for following him, while Absalom bears the greater guilt for deceiving them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase "stole the hearts" as a moral verdict on Absalom's campaign. What is gained by deception is theft, and the narrator signals that this kingdom is built on a lie.

verses.text: At the end of forty years, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes: WEB reads "at the end of forty years"; some ancient versions read four, and some interpreters prefer that. Arminian readers note that Absalom uses a religious vow as cover for rebellion, abusing sacred language.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the textual question without forcing an answer. They emphasize that Absalom's appeal to a vow to the LORD is hypocrisy, using worship as a mask for treason.

verses.text: For your servant vowed a vow while I stayed at Geshur in Syria, saying, ‘If the LORD shall indeed bring me again to Jerusalem, then I will serve the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom claims he vowed in Geshur to serve the LORD if brought back to Jerusalem. Arminian readers see deceit that exploits David's love and piety, a son using his father's faith against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Absalom fled to Geshur after killing Amnon (13:38). His claim of a vow to serve the LORD rings hollow against his actions, showing how sin can borrow the language of devotion.

verses.text: The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he arose and went to Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes: David says, "Go in peace." Arminian readers see the pathos of a father who blesses his son without suspicion, a reminder that David's failures as a father have made him vulnerable to this betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony of "peace" spoken to one plotting war. David's blessing is sincere, yet God's discipline is unfolding through the very son he trusts.

verses.text: But Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then you shall say, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom sends agents through the tribes to proclaim him king in Hebron at the trumpet's sound. Arminian readers see a carefully planned coup, the fruit of long, deliberate choices to grasp at power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hebron was where David was first made king (2 Samuel 5:3). Absalom stages his rebellion in a place of royal significance, seeking to claim what God had given to his father.

verses.text: Two hundred men went with Absalom out of Jerusalem, who were invited, and went in their simplicity; and they didn’t know anything.
verses.arminianNotes: Two hundred men go with Absalom "in their simplicity" and "didn't know anything." Arminian readers note that the innocent are drawn into a plot they did not choose, showing how deception spreads guilt and danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how the unsuspecting become instruments of another's scheme. The narrator distinguishes these men from the conspirators, a reminder that God judges hearts and motives, not appearances alone.

verses.text: Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he was offering the sacrifices. The conspiracy was strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel, David's counselor, joins the conspiracy, and "the people increased continually." Arminian readers see betrayal by a trusted advisor, a choice that strengthens the revolt and deepens David's grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahithophel's defection gives the rebellion strength. Many connect Psalm 41:9, "my own familiar friend," to experiences like this, which Jesus applies to his betrayer in John 13:18.
